result: The authors developed an open-source automated high-resolution fluorescence microscope based on the UC2 toolbox, combining low-cost components with high-quality optics and integrated software. The system is modular, cost-effective, and all designs are openly accessible.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core contribution. The editor states the study provides 'compelling evidence' that the UC2 framework can be expanded for single-molecule localization microscopy. Reviewer 2 notes the system 'has great potential' and praises the accessibility. Reviewer 3 describes this as 'compelling work' and highlights the 'tight integration of hardware and software.'

result: The microscope demonstrates high-resolution fluorescence imaging of fixed samples, with even illumination across the field of view (variations up to 25%) and diffraction-limited imaging of cellular structures like microtubules.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the presented experimental data is convincing' and lists this capability among the demonstrated features. The reviewers do not question the quality of the widefield imaging data or the illumination homogeneity measurements.

result: The microscope enables long-term live-cell imaging over several days when operated inside an incubator, with cells exhibiting normal morphology and growth. The system shows negligible drift and maintains stability even on a wetlab bench with foam damping.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms the system demonstrates 'extended live cell imaging both using bright-field and fluorescence in the incubator.' The editor notes the authors 'managed to fit the instrumentation and control thereof in a unit that can be placed in a small stage-top-incubator.' No concerns are raised about these claims.

result: The microscope reaches single-molecule sensitivity and enables single-particle tracking experiments in cells, with the ability to generate trajectories and extract diffusion parameters that agree with previous observations.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly lists 'single-particle tracking of quantum dots' among the convincing experimental demonstrations. The editor affirms the system can 'rival the capabilities of comparable commercial instruments.' No reviewer questions the single-particle tracking data or analysis.

result: The microscope performs SMLM super-resolution microscopy (dSTORM) in cells, achieving a resolution of 93 nm as measured by Fourier ring correlation, with the ability to resolve the characteristic 'railroad track' pattern of microtubules with 38-43 nm spacing.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms 'STORM measurements in cells stained against tubulin' as convincing experimental data. The editor states the study provides 'compelling evidence' for single-molecule localization microscopy capability. No concerns are raised about the super-resolution data quality or resolution measurements.

result: The system costs a fraction of commercial counterparts while providing comparable data quality and capabilities, allowing sophisticated imaging assays to be performed at a professional level with greatly reduced cost.
evaluation: The editor explicitly states the 'UC.STORM setup can rival the capabilities of comparable commercial instruments at a fraction of the costs.' Reviewer 3 notes the system uses 'cost-effective alternatives' and describes the work as 'compelling.' No reviewer challenges the cost-effectiveness or data quality comparisons.

result: The microscope can be assembled and operated by lay users with minimal background knowledge in optics, electronics, and informatics, providing proof of concept that high-quality scientific data can be generated with a low-budget system and open-source software.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the microscope is specifically designed to work with incubators and can image cells in culture over long periods' and that it is 'easily accessible to scientists, students, and the general public.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'added plenty of information on the GitHub page that should make it significantly easier for interested researchers to replicate the instrument.'

result: The emission pathway uses an Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera that is 30-60 times more affordable than conventional scientific cameras, while being more compact and consuming less energy, though with lower quantum efficiency.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the authors 'combined a cheapish laser, detector and x,y,(z) stage with expensive filters/dichroics and an expensive high-end objective.' The cost comparison and camera characteristics are not questioned by any reviewer.

result: The system uses ImSwitch software for control and acquisition, with integrated microEye algorithms for online SMLM reconstruction, automation features, and access to Napari plugins for direct data analysis.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly identifies 'the tight integration of the hardware and the software (namely the implementations of imSwitch as a GUI to control data acquisition, OS SMLM algorithms for fast sub-pixel localisation and access to Napari)' as a strength of the manuscript. No concerns are raised about the software implementation.

result: The microscope shows drift of less than 1 μm over 2 hours when imaging fluorescent beads, indicating suitability for experiments requiring repeated measurements of the same field of view.
evaluation: This stability measurement is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is implicitly accepted as part of the 'convincing' experimental data package. No concerns are raised about drift measurements or stability claims.

result: The system uses injection-molded UC2 cubes that provide significantly higher manufacturing precision than 3D-printed versions, resulting in greater mechanical stability and reproducibility while being available at low cost through mass production, making the setup portable and reproducible.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors used injection-moulded blocks that will have a limited availability if not offered commercially by a third party,' raising a concern about the practical accessibility of this component. While the technical advantages are not disputed, the reviewer questions whether this limits the open-source nature of the system.

result: The system can be used for routine imaging in laboratories without means to acquire commercial systems, can serve as teaching material for students, facilitates use in remote areas, and makes high-quality imaging accessible to research groups with limited monetary means in lower-income countries.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the authors' work will make scientific instruments more accessible and remove obstacles to the free diffusion of capabilities and know-how in science' and that it will 'enable more people to conduct scientific research.' Reviewer 3 describes the work as 'helping to make super-resolved microscopy more accessible.' These potential applications are affirmed rather than questioned.

result: The main limitation is the requirement of a high-NA objective (the most expensive component at >15k Euros), which cannot be replaced for scientific imaging, though low-cost objective quality is improving.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the system 'combined a cheapish laser, detector and x,y,(z) stage with expensive filters/dichroics and an expensive high-end objective (>15k Euros),' acknowledging this cost limitation. The necessity of the high-quality objective is implicitly accepted by all reviewers.
